hero.caption: Inside view of the stage hall planned by Berlin-based renowned architect Bruno Ahrends (1878–1948) for progressive boading school Schule am Meer (School by the Sea) on the East Frisian island Juist in Prussia. Students and teachers alike are costumed on stage with its elevated pedestals to the left and to the right. Standing in the stage's center Swiss teacher Rudolf Aeschlimann (1884–1961, with a pole) and 5 positions from him to the right deputy headmaster Dr. Paul Reiner (1886–1932) from Middle Franconia in Bavaria can be recognized. The building was unique in German Reich, the only free-standing theater hall of any private or state-run school (until today).

images.filename: Juist schule am meer 1929.png
images.caption: Drawing of Schule am Meer on the East Frisian island of Juist in the Free State of Prussia in German Reich. Due to the stage of expansion the drawing can be dated to summer 1928. One building on the far left and three on the far right are not related to S.a.M. The viewer of this drawing looks northbound, so the beach and the North Sea are in the upper part behind the dune range. Its lower part (southbound) sports the boathouse near Wadden Sea and the barn for livestock of the boarding school. A dingy sails in front of the boathouse in the Wadden Sea. On the barns right is the Duck Pond (its remnants today named: Alder Pond) which the younger students used to raft on. The smaller posts which can be recognized are related to electricity and telephone, the higher posts all flag posts. The boarding school's flagpost is shaped like a Christian cross with plus two sidearms. Each comradeship had a pennant which was raised and pulled down acc. to the presence of the individual comradeship, so during vacations usually all were down. Same with the boarding school's flag. There also had been an obligation to raise the German national flag, the Prussian flag plus after Jan 30, 1933 the Nazi swastika flag. The drawing indicates the locations of a few of the eleven vegetable gardens the students and teachers had layed out. All gardens including the school's botanical garden had to be secured against the steadily moving sand of the dunes and some cows so they got fenced. All the dunes had to be fixed with sods / turf divots, a nearly daily task for students and teachers alike.

images.filename: Ahrends bruno buehnenhalle schule am meer 1929.png
images.caption:
Sketch of the construction project Bühnenhalle of Schule am Meer (= School by the Sea) on the East Frisian island Juist in Prussia, based on the status of plans in 1929. The sketch, named Schule in Juist (= School in Juist) was made by Berlin-based renowned architect Bruno Ahrends (1878–1948) whose buildings are mostly under monument protection today, some even classified as UNESCO world cultural heritage. Most of his buildings are in Berlin, few in the German states of Hesse and Lower Saxony.
The sketch represents a southwesterly view. In the background of the sketch you will recognize the North Sea, but Ahrends left out the northern chain of dunes of the island which separates the school buildings from the wide beach and the sea. The foreground of the sketch at that time indicates an unattached landscape of dunes with beach grass only. In this environment the planned ensemble seems a bit strange as it radiates a metropolitan charisma.
On the right you can see a square tower which was planned including a flat, maybe a Duplex, for the school's headmaster Martin Luserke and his family. An interesting detail is that the tower was meant to bear an equally narrow vertical window band at its southerly side, like the realized stage hall itself (see picture at Wikimedia Commons) at its northerly side. The same narrow vertical window band can be recognized close to the interior angle of the L-shaped building on the left, right in the implied hard shadow of the drawing. Actually it is unknown if the lower part of the tower was planned to serve for the adjacent stage hall which on this sketch can be recognized right behind the tower. The accessible flat roof of the tower was planned with a balustrade and the school's flagpole, formed as a Christian cross. It hoisted the school flag with its logo as well as smaller burgees with the signets of the nine comradeships which were mixed groups of about ten pupils of different age (10 to circa 19-year-olds) and sex with their comradeship leader, a teacher. On top of the stage hall were signal lamps for the school's sailing dinghys to allow them to navigate home. These signal lamps would have been placed on top of the tower if it would have been carried out. The external flue of the stage hall would have been bricked up to jut out over the tower. This is shown in the contemporary 3D model by Ahrends and also in his monochrome sketch of the northerly front (see both pictures at Wikimedia Commons). Today the existing flue indicates ecactly the square tower's dimensions and where it would have been placed.

The mirrored L-shaped building on the left was meant as living quarters (flats/apartments) for teachers in its western (left) wing and classrooms in its eastern (right) wing which was planned 90° offset. Between the buildings a square atrium-like courtyard was intended. It was meant to be roofed in its fringe area and could have been used as entrée for public performances in the stage hall and as schoolyard. The roof of this fringe area in the square atrium-like courtyard was necessary for protection against stormy weather conditions, rain and snowfall. The compound of this architectonical ensemble seems to be completely bounded by a wall which probably was meant to serve against the moving sand. This wall (or artificial dune) can also be recognized in the contemporary 3D model by Ahrends and also in his monochrome sketch of the northerly front (see picture at Wikimedia Commons).

images.filename: Theaterszene schule am meer juist.jpg
images.caption: Scene from a play in the stage hall of the progressive boarding-school Schule am Meer (School by the Sea) on the East Frisian island of Juist in Prussia, built in 1930/31 by the Berlin-based renowned architect Bruno Ahrends (1878–1948). With such plays performed in German, partly also in English and French, the S.a.M. during school holidays went on tour to professional stages in major German cities. They received excellent reviews from professional theater critics. With regard to the foreign languages, not only the subject teachers but also native-speaking pupils and students from England and France provided support. The literary, musicologist and critic Hans Mayer (1907-2001) in 1979 wrote about Luserke's Shakespeare play Twelfth Night, Or what you will performance with his S.a.M. students in Cologne at the end of the 1920s: “I have never seen the beautiful work more graceful and cheerful. Every performance since then, including a festival performance in Salzburg, must fade away. The canon Shut up, you dog was irresistible. Youth and grace still in rudeness”. The Austrian actress Maria Fein characterized headmaster Martin Luserke as a "genius of the theater" (Theatergenie) when she was visiting a stage-play in Juist.

images.filename: Bruno ahrends hallenbau schule am meer loog juist 1930-31.png
images.caption: In 1929 Bruno Ahrends (1878–1948) projected the theater hall of Schule am Meer (= School by the Sea) on the German island of Juist which was erected in 1930/31. The ground-breaking ceremony was held on 3 May 1930 which also marked the 50th birthday of the school's founder Martin Luserke (1880–1968). The official house opening was at Pentecost/Whitsun weekend 1931. At that time the Hallenbau was the largest concrete building in East Frisia, Prussia. It included a large theater hall with stage and gallery which also was used for indoor sports classes in wintertime. At the beginning of the 1950s the building was completely modificated for a children's home named Inselburg (= island's castle). So since then it's not in its original state. The former theater hall became a second floor while the gallery and the stage were aborted. The building became more windows, but the long slim vertical strip of ribbon windows was closed with masonry. Today the building is part of the youth hostel of Juist.

images.filename: Aerial view schule am meer juist 1929.png
images.caption: Historical aerial view dated 1929 of Schule am Meer on the East Frisian island of Juist which is located between Wadden Sea and North Sea. The picture was made from a plane which passed along the southern coast of the rather narrow island. In the background the wide beach to the North Sea can be recognized where the S.a.M. students regularly performed athletics, football (soccer), field hockey and the like. Temporarily it also served as an airfield. The students took a bath in the Sea early in the mornings right after gymnastics in the dunes, not only in spring and summer but until December. Still no student got urged to by their teachers. From the left to the right: Cut-off at the left edge of the picture a light wooden barrack may get noticed which is part of a western annex to the high-roofed brick building named do. This wooden barrack was named mi, while the northern wooden barrack behind the high-roofed brick building was named re. mi contained the natural sciences including 30 sea aquariums plus an apartment for musician Eduard Zuckmayer. do sported two apartments for the teacher families Martin Luserke and Fritz Hafner plus first aid and sickbay of the boarding school. re contained two classrooms which were also used for boxing and dancing classes. The whitish smaller buildings on dos right in the past had been islander's homes which S.a.M. used to house teachers. In the picture's center the compound of S.a.M. got surrounded by four buildings: the main building named Diesseits (The Here and Now) in the north with a high roof and two annexes to the east and the south, the dark residential wooden barrack Jenseits (The Beyond) in the south, the whitish Westfalenhalle (Westphalia Hall) in the east sporting a high chimney/smokestack and Arche (Arch) in the west, the latter a laterally reversed L-shaped brick building with an attic. The main building Diesseits housed an apartment for the teacher family Aeschlimann, rooms for middle school girls, the kitchen and the dining-room in its eastern annex. The residential barrack Jenseits housed about 45 middle school boys and teachers while the residential brick building Arche (L) housed the seniors, a single female teacher and its southern part the apartment of the teacher family Reiner. Its attic housed the senior girls, its first floor the senior boys. So all who graduated at Schule am Meer before lived in the Arche building. Westfalenhalle contained the wash house, bathtubs, showers, washbasins/sinks and workshops like a locksmithery and a carpentry. Its annexes to the north and east contained coal and wood inventory, those to the south other stock. South of Westfalenhalle is the school's white flag post shaped like a Christian cross. It sported the German national flag, then horizontally striped in black-white-red, the Prussian flag, horizontally striped in black and white and the up to nine pennants of the comradeships, of different colors, sporting a logo acc. to their names. After Jan 30, 1933 also the Nazi swastika flag was ordered to raise. South of Arche two wooden buildings for livestock can be recognized, the larger named Olymp. They housed a horse, pigs and poultry. South of it (not on this picture) the boathouse of the boarding school was erected in 1927 to house dinghys and a larger sailboat with engine. The three buildings on the right of the picture are islander's homes, the largest at the picture's right edge includes a café and restaurant named Zur freien Aussicht (= Unhindered lookout).

images.filename: Dr Paul Reiner 1886–1932.png
images.caption: Paul Reiner, a chemist and highschool teacher who in 1913 started as a tutor in the family of Edgar Jaffé (1866–1921) and his wife Elisabeth Frieda Amélie Sophie (1874–1973), née as Freiin von Richthofen in Wolfratshausen, Kingdom of Bavaria. After WWI he taught from 1919 at German progressive boarding-school Freie Schulgemeinde (Free School Community) of Wickersdorf near Saalfeld in Thuringia Forest and from 1925 at progressive boarding-school Schule am Meer (School by the Sea) on the East Frisian island Juist in Prussia where he also served as deputy headmaster of Martin Luserke (1880–1968).

images.filename: Ellen abel-musgrave maria becker juist schule am mer 1929-30.jpg
images.caption: Ellen Abel-Musgrave (center, 1908–1988) was born in Clifton near Bristol in England. She served as a gymnastics teacher after she completed her training at Dora Menzler school in Leipzig and Wustrow in 1929. In 1929/30 she was part of the staff of progressive Schule am Meer (= School by the Sea) on the East-Frisian island Juist in Prussia. The school's headmaster was Martin Luserke (1880–1968). Ellen Abel-Musgrave was the older sister of internationally renowned economist Richard Abel Musgrave (1910–2007) and the daughter of writer and translator Curt Abel-Musgrave (1860–1938). On the right: Maria Becker (* 28 January, 1920 in Berlin, Prussia, German Reich; † 5 September, 2012 in Uster, Canton Zürich, Switzerland), daughter of the German actor Theodor Becker (* 18 February, 1880 in Mannheim; † 26 June, 1952 in Coppenbrügge) and his second wife, the Austrian actress Maria Fein (born on 7 April, 1892 in Vienna; deceased on 15 September, 1965 in Zürich, Switzerland). The girl on the left hasn't been identified, yet. All three are sitting on the beach of the North Sea in the north of the boarding-school's compound.

images.filename: Do martin luserke fritz hafner loog juist.jpg
images.caption: The building on the East Frisian island Juist in Prussia had been the home of the Doyen family until it was bought by the Schule am Meer Foundation (Stiftung Schule am Meer). It got partially demolished and was built up again in a larger scale in 1927, internally named as do. Its first floor apt became the home of the Hafner family (Fritz Hafner, 1877–1964), the apt on second floor became home of the Luserke family (Martin Luserke, 1880–1968), while other rooms were used to house the sickbay and the first aid post of progressive boarding-school Schule am Meer. A wooden barrack named re containing two classrooms was attached to the north, a wooden barrack named mi was attached to the west to house Eduard Zuckmayer (1890–1972). Do-re-mi, see Solmization).

images.filename: Buehnenhalle schule am meer.jpg
images.caption: Interior view of the theatre hall of Schule am Meer on the East Frisian island of Juist in Prussia, erected by Berlin-based architect Bruno Ahrends (1878–1948). Costumed teachers and students include as 2nd from the left (sitting): Eduard Zuckmayer (1890–1972). Behind him standing: Anni Reiner (1891–1972), née Hochschild. On her left her husband Dr. Paul Reiner (1886–1932). In the front row standing on the right is principal Martin Luserke (1880–1968). Slightly left of the picture's centre stands the student Ulrich Sild (1911–1937), bare torso, wearing a necklace and a headband.

images.filename: Buehnenhalle schule am meer loog juist.jpg
images.caption: Interior view of the stage hall of progressive boarding school Schule am Meer (School by the Sea) on the East Frisian island Juist. The stage hall was planned by renowned Berlin-based Jewish architect Bruno Ahrends (1878–1948) and erected in 1930/31. Students and teachers in costumes on stage. Far left in the back headmaster Martin Luserke. The building nationwide was the one and only free-standing stage hall of a school.

images.filename: Arche schule am meer loog juist.jpg
images.caption: Das Wohngebäude Arche auf dem Areal des reformpädagogischen Landerziehungsheims Schule am Meer im Loog auf der ostfriesischen Insel Juist in Preußen. Die Arche wurde im Jahr 1927 errichtet, Architekt war vermutlich Josef Rings (1878–1957), dessen Sohn Werner Rings (1910–1998) vom 21. April 1926 bis zum 21. März 1929 (Abitur) die Schule am Meer besuchte. Die Arche beherbergte die Primaner, im Erdgeschoss die Jungen, im Dachgeschoss die Mädchen, jeweils in Einzelzimmern. Darin wohnten beispielsweise Felicitas Kestner (1914–2001, verh. Kukuck), Rolf Pappiér (1914–1998, nach Emigration Ralph Pappier), Werner Rings und Jens Rohwer (1914–1994). Im südlichen Teil der spiegelbildlich L-förmigen Arche lebte die Familie Dr. Paul Reiner (1886–1932) mit Ehefrau Anna Sara Reiner (1891–1972), geb. Hochschild und deren zuletzt vier Töchter Renate (1917–2003), Eva Maria (1919–1999), Ruth Elisabeth (1922–1948) und Karin (* 1931), außerdem die Lehrerin Leonore Luise Neumann (1879–1939), die im Gebäude Neufundland die jüngsten Schüler betreute. – Zum Zeitpunkt dieser frühen Aufnahme standen auf der hier abgebildeten östlichen Längsseite noch keine gemauerten Sitzbänke mit Holz-Sitzfläche an der Hauswand.
